app.name: X (formerly Twitter) API v2 developer app

verdict.summary: Composio has no managed X OAuth app, so you must create your own X developer account, buy pay-per-use credits, and register an app. Setup itself is quick; the uncertainty is X's use-case review for wider access, which has no published timeline, and several API scopes Composio requests are no longer available on self-serve tiers.
verdict.hands_on_effort: 1-2 hours of active work, plus time to fund credits and write the use-case and privacy text
verdict.time_to_first_connection: About 1 hour after your developer account is verified (account verification timing was not found)
verdict.approval_wait: Unknown. A legacy Elevated access process was reported at up to two weeks; community threads describe waits of weeks to months with no published SLA.

gates.name: Your own developer account and app (no review)
gates.unlocks: Create the app, enable OAuth 2.0, get a Client ID and secret, and connect your own X account through Composio.
limits: Pay-per-use: you buy credits in the Developer Console; there is no subscription and no free tier for new developers
Maximum of 10 Apps per account (support page); the policy text allows 3 apps per service (dev, staging, production)
Access tokens last 2 hours unless offline.access is requested, in which case a refresh token is issued
Authorization codes expire 30 seconds after issue
Developer account is limited to one per X user
gates.time_to_reach: Minutes to about an hour after the developer account is verified and credits are funded

gates.name: No separate invited-user mode found in the sources
gates.unlocks: Not established. The sources describe no test-user allowlist or unlisted install mode for OAuth apps. Other users of your app are governed by the same pay-per-use access as Gate 1 unless X says otherwise.
limits: Per-app request limit for Tweet and user lookup is 900 requests per 15 minutes under OAuth 2.0
Posting limits reported by a third party: 100 posts per 15 minutes per user, 10,000 per 24 hours per app
Free scaled access exists only for Public Utility apps and is handled case by case; it is not self-serve
Apps can be limited for alleged policy violations with no reason sent

gates.name: Public use after X reviews your use case
gates.unlocks: Other X users can authorize your app for public use, subject to X's review of your proposed use.
limits: X reviews every proposed use of the developer platform
The use-case text you submit is binding; substantive changes need X approval first
Apps rejected for compliance reasons cannot be reopened; pending apps can be reopened by replying to X's email
No X app marketplace or directory listing review was found
gates.time_to_reach: Unknown. Legacy Elevated review was reported at up to two weeks; community reports describe weeks to months.

steps.title: Create an X developer account
steps.detail: Sign in at the developer portal with an X account. Verify your email, enter developer name, location and use case, accept the developer agreement, then verify the account from the email you receive before the portal opens. Google or Apple sign-in users may need to add a contact email and phone.
gotchas: A single X user can have only one developer account; if you already have one, use it rather than creating another.
Email and phone verification on the X account may be required before you can apply.
The dashboard redirects signed-out visitors to an X login page.

steps.title: Fund pay-per-use credits
steps.detail: Open the Developer Console at console.x.com and buy credits. There is no free tier for new developers, so API calls will fail without credits. New pay-per-use accounts may earn one-time free credits after saving a payment card and after the first successful auto-recharge; these expire 3 months after grant.
gotchas: Credits expire 3 months after they are granted.
Free-credit amounts are as announced in X's October 2, 2026 changelog; check the console for what applies to your account.

steps.title: Create the app and write its description
steps.detail: In the Developer Console, create a new App. Give it a clear name. Enter a use-case description that matches what the app will actually do, because X treats it as binding. The App description may be shown publicly if the app offers Sign in with X, so write it for public reading. An agent can draft the text for you to review and paste.

values.label: App name
values.value: Your product name (clearly labeled, e.g. 'Acme Agent - Dev')

gotchas: Each App needs a use-case description; X will not approve Apps without one.
Use one App per use case. Do not register several apps for the same use case.
Keep dev and production apps separate and clearly labeled; development or staging apps may not serve production.

steps.title: Turn on OAuth 2.0 and choose the app type
steps.detail: Open the App's settings and go to the authentication settings. Enable OAuth 2.0. Until you do this, no Client ID appears under Keys and Tokens. Pick the app type: Web App and Automated App or bot receive a client secret (confidential clients); Native App and Single page App do not (public clients). For a server-side token exchange such as Composio's, a Web App is the likely fit; confirm this with Composio's X setup notes.

values.label: App type
values.value: Web App (confidential, receives Client Secret) unless Composio documents otherwise

gotchas: Changing the app type later may change which credentials you get; choose it before you copy keys.

steps.title: Add the Composio callback URL
steps.detail: In the App's authentication settings, add a Callback URL. The redirect_uri in every authorize request must exactly match one saved here. Paste the exact callback URL shown in your Composio auth config. Composio's default is listed in the open questions; use the value Composio displays for your auth config.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: Matching is exact. A trailing slash or a different host (backend.composio.dev vs. another path) will fail.
Sources list two different Composio callback URLs; register the one your Composio auth config shows.

steps.title: Copy the Client ID and Client Secret into Composio
steps.detail: Under Keys and Tokens, copy the OAuth 2.0 Client ID and Client Secret. In Composio, create the X (twitter) auth config using your own credentials instead of a managed app. Store the secret only in Composio or your secret manager; never commit it.
gotchas: Composio offers no managed OAuth for X, so this step cannot be skipped.
No OpenID discovery document is served at x.com; use the endpoints above from the docs.

steps.title: Trim the scope list before authorizing
steps.detail: Composio's default list includes follow, like and some DM and list scopes. X removed API following and likes from all self-serve tiers, so request only the scopes your agent needs. Include offline.access if you need a refresh token. Scopes are space-separated in the authorize request.

values.label: Add only if needed
values.value: tweet.write dm.read dm.write list.read list.write bookmark.read bookmark.write media.write

gotchas: follow, like and quote-post endpoints are removed from self-serve tiers; requesting follows.write or like.write will not give working calls.
Whether Composio's default scopes are grantable to new pay-per-use apps is unverified; test with the trimmed list first.

steps.title: Run a test authorization with your own account
steps.detail: Using Composio, start the connect flow for the X auth config and sign in with your own X account. Approve the trimmed scopes. Confirm a token is returned and make one read call (for example, users.read on your own account). Expect the access token to last 2 hours unless offline.access was granted.
gotchas: Authorization codes expire 30 seconds after issue; the exchange must happen quickly.
The authorize page loads even with an invalid client_id; a bad client ID is caught only after login.

steps.title: Draft and host the privacy policy and consent text
steps.detail: An agent can draft a privacy policy covering what you collect, how it is shared (including with X), and how users can make requests. You must host it at a public URL and show it to people before they download, install or sign up. Authenticating into your service is not consent; add an explicit consent step before the app posts or follows for a user.
gotchas: The privacy policy must be visible before sign-up, not only in the app footer after login.
Sign in with X must be at least as prominent as other sign-in options; never ask for a user's X password.

steps.title: Check automation and data-use rules
steps.detail: An agent can produce a compliance checklist for your app. If the app posts as a bot, enable the 'Automated' profile label, disclose the operator in the bio, and link to a human-managed account. Confirm the app uses only the official API (no browser automation), does not train AI or ML models on X data (Grok excepted), deletes X content within 24 hours of a deletion request, and keeps usage records for audit.
gotchas: Browser automation or scraping of X is a permanent suspension offense regardless of tier.
X may audit compliance once per year.

steps.title: Stay within rate and redistribution limits
steps.detail: Set your client to respect per-app and per-user limits and back off on 429 responses. Do not circumvent limits by spreading calls across apps. If the app will redistribute X post IDs, keep it under 1,500,000 Post IDs per entity per 30 days unless X gives written permission.
gotchas: Limits reported by third parties may be out of date; check the console for current values.

steps.title: Submit the use case for X review
steps.detail: Submit the app for access through the developer console or support channel X provides, using the use-case text from step 3. Free scaled access is only for Public Utility apps and is a case-by-case manual review; if you are not a public or government service, expect to move to pay-per-use. Keep a copy of the submission and everything X replies.
gotchas: Public Utility free access is reserved for government or public services; the Enterprise tier is listed for government use, and the sources do not resolve this conflict.
Do not change the use case after submission without X's approval.

steps.title: Wait for X's review
steps.detail: X reviews each proposed use. No published SLA was found. Community reports describe applications pending for weeks or months with no reply. If the application is rejected for compliance reasons it cannot be reopened; if it is still pending, reply to X's email to reopen it.
gotchas: Do not build a launch date on the legacy two-week Elevated figure; it may not apply to the current model.
Do not ship public sign-up until approval is confirmed.

blockers.symptom: Following, liking and quote-posting endpoints return errors or are unavailable for the app.
blockers.cause: Removed from all self-serve tiers (Apr 2026); like and follow POST endpoints were removed from Free in Aug 2025.
blockers.fix: Remove follow and like scopes from the request; redesign features that need them or plan for a different tier.

blockers.symptom: Programmatic replies via POST /2/tweets are refused.
blockers.cause: Since Feb 23, 2026, replies are only allowed when the original author has summoned the replier; applies to self-serve tiers.
blockers.fix: Do not build auto-reply features unless the original author has summoned the app.

blockers.symptom: App is limited for alleged policy violations; no reason is given.
blockers.cause: Community reports describe limits applied without a reason being sent to the account.
blockers.fix: Check the policy and guidelines, stop the flagged behavior, and contact X support through the developer console.
blockers.contact: X developer support via the developer console or support pages

blockers.symptom: Application stays pending for weeks or months with no reply.
blockers.cause: Community threads report slow review with no published SLA.
blockers.fix: Reply to X's email to reopen a pending request; plan launch without a fixed date.
blockers.contact: Reply to X's email about the pending application

blockers.symptom: Access request rejected for compliance reasons.
blockers.cause: X's review found the proposed use non-compliant.
blockers.fix: The rejection cannot be reopened; review the policy and submit a new, compliant app only if it is not a duplicate of the same use case.

composio.note: Composio has no managed OAuth app for X, so you must bring your own X OAuth 2.0 Client ID and secret. Start on your own app now. Trim the default scopes: follow and like scopes are removed from self-serve tiers. Authorize URL: https://x.com/i/oauth2/authorize; token URL: https://api.x.com/2/oauth2/token.

evidence.claim: Composio has no managed OAuth app for X; the developer must supply their own OAuth 2.0 client ID and secret.
evidence.quote: "managed_auth_schemes": [], "managed_oauth_available": false

evidence.claim: Developer Guidelines table says government use requires an Enterprise tier, which may conflict with the Public Utility free-access route; the mismatch is unresolved in the sources.
evidence.quote: Government use | Requires Enterprise tier

evidence.claim: October 2, 2026 changelog: pay-per-use accounts can earn one-time free credits: $20 for saving a first eligible payment card and up to $50 matching the first successful auto-recharge; credits expire 3 months after grant.
evidence.quote: a one-time **$20** when an account saves its first eligible payment card

evidence.claim: The Developer Policy says X reviews every proposed use of the developer platform, and developers must disclose planned use to be granted and to keep access.
evidence.quote: We review all proposed uses of the X developer platform to verify policy compliance

evidence.claim: The use-case description submitted during developer signup is binding; a substantive deviation requires X's approval before the new use begins, or access may be suspended.
evidence.quote: Your use case description is binding on you

evidence.claim: The developer account support page says applications rejected for compliance reasons cannot be reopened, while those pending can be reopened by replying to X's email.
evidence.quote: Access requests rejected for compliance reasons cannot be reopened.

evidence.claim: Developer Policy requires a privacy policy to be shown before users download, install or sign up, and it must disclose what is collected, how it is shared (including with X), and how to make requests.
evidence.quote: You must display your service's privacy policy to people before they are permitted to download, install, or sign up to your service.

evidence.claim: Developer Policy says authenticating into a service is not by itself consent; express and informed consent is needed before any action is taken on a user's behalf, including posting or following.
evidence.quote: Please note that a person authenticating into your service does not by itself constitute consent.

evidence.claim: Developer Policy caps a developer at three applications for development, staging and production of the same service, registered to one account and clearly labeled; development or staging apps may not serve production.
evidence.quote: you may create and use a maximum of 3 applications for development, staging, and production instances of the same service.

evidence.claim: The support page separately says an account is limited to 10 Apps to combat spam and multi-key abuse; more require a case through the API Policy Support Form with a use case for each app.
evidence.quote: We have limited accounts to a maximum of 10 Apps as an important step to combat spam and multi-key abuse.

evidence.claim: Developer Policy prohibits white-label versions of an app unless X is notified and approves separately, and prohibits registering multiple apps for one use case.
evidence.quote: You may not register multiple applications for a single use case or substantially similar or overlapping use cases.

evidence.claim: Account path is pay-per-use: credits are bought in the Developer Console at console.x.com, with no subscription and no free tier for new developers.
evidence.quote: You buy credits in the Developer Console at console.x.com

evidence.claim: Developer Guidelines treat scraping and browser automation as a permanent suspension offense; only the official API is permitted, regardless of tier.
evidence.quote: App scrapes X via browser automation (not API) | Permanent suspension—API only

evidence.claim: Developer Guidelines prohibit storing X data to train AI or ML models, except Grok.
evidence.quote: App stores X data to train AI/ML models | Prohibited (except Grok)

evidence.claim: Automated accounts must enable the Automated profile label, disclose the operator in the bio, and link to a human-managed account.
evidence.quote: Enable the 'Automated' profile label

evidence.claim: Deletion deadlines: X content must be deleted within 24 hours of an X or user deletion request, and within 10 business days when API access is terminated.
evidence.quote: Your API access is terminated | **10 business days** (must delete all X data)

evidence.claim: X may audit compliance up to once per year, and developers must keep records of how they use X data.
evidence.quote: X may audit your compliance

evidence.claim: Developer Policy says the App description is shown publicly when an app implements Sign in with X, so it should be reviewed before launch.
evidence.quote: your App's description will be displayed publicly

evidence.claim: Developer Policy requires Sign in with X to be at least as prominent as other sign-in options, and it bars requesting a user's X password or consumer key.

evidence.claim: Developer Policy requires that API rate limits are not exceeded or circumvented.

evidence.claim: The docs label no scope as sensitive, restricted or subject to separate review; the only gating visible in the docs is the app's enabled permissions and access tier.

evidence.quote: Following, Likes, and Quote-Posts via the API have been removed from all self-serve tiers.

open_questions: No official X app marketplace or directory listing requirements or timelines were found.
Official docs for current console.x.com app-creation fields (privacy policy URL, terms URL, app icon) were not retrieved; check the form when creating the app.
No source says whether any scope needs separate review, a security assessment or a privacy policy; sensitive or restricted scope lists are unknown.
Current review time for a standard pay-per-use app is unconfirmed; the timelines found come from the legacy Elevated process.
No install or user caps, and no test-user allowlist or unlisted mode, were found for unreviewed OAuth apps.
App-count limit conflicts: 3 apps per service in the policy versus 10 per account on the support page; the support page may be partly stale.
Composio's default scopes include follow, like and DM write scopes; whether new pay-per-use apps can be granted them is unverified.

Composio's configured redirect URI (backend.composio.dev/api/v1/auth-apps/add) differs from the callback in the probe (backend.composio.dev/api/v3/toolkits/auth/callback); confirm which one your auth config shows before registering.
Whether the developer account verification step has a review delay is not stated in the sources.
Government/Public Utility free access conflicts with the Enterprise tier requirement in the Developer Guidelines; unresolved.
